provider_metadata.assistant_note: The surgery confirmed the diagnosis. A migrated biliary stent was lodged in a Meckel diverticulum and had perforated the nearby ileum, causing purulent peritonitis and small-bowel obstruction. About 20 cm of bowel was removed, the ends were rejoined, and the abdomen was washed out and drained. IV piperacillin-tazobactam was ordered, but her allergies and kidney function were not documented and still need checking. I'm sending her to the surgical ward with close monitoring and clear triggers for ICU escalation.

args.urgency: urgent — admit to the surgical ward straight after the operation, with close monitoring
args.rationale: She has had emergency surgery that removed the source of infection: laparoscopy converted to open surgery, removal of about 20 cm of small bowel including the Meckel diverticulum with the migrated biliary stent and the perforation, a side-to-side join of the bowel, washout and drains. Purulent peritonitis was found. She is 70 and has type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, chronic atrial fibrillation and COPD. That puts her at high risk after surgery for a leak where the bowel was joined, an abscess in the abdomen, sepsis, rapid atrial fibrillation, lung complications and blood sugar problems. Her vital signs and blood tests were not documented at presentation. She needs close monitoring, with a low threshold to move her to the ICU or high-dependency unit if she becomes unstable.
args.followup_or_handoff: Handoff to the surgical team. (1) Continue IV piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g every 6 hours. Confirm she has no beta-lactam allergy, adjust the dose to her kidney function once creatinine is known, send peritoneal fluid cultures, and give a short course of about 4 days after source control. (2) Nothing by mouth with a nasogastric tube at first. Give IV fluids, measure urine output, and use analgesia that avoids NSAIDs until her kidney function is known. Add breathing exercises and bronchodilators for COPD. (3) Check full blood count, kidney function and electrolytes, lactate, CRP and blood clotting tests. Start sliding-scale insulin for diabetes. Do a 12-lead ECG and use telemetry for atrial fibrillation. (4) Review the drains every day. Watch for signs of an anastomotic leak or abscess (fever, rising inflammatory markers, worsening tenderness, abnormal drain fluid). Get a repeat CT if there is concern. (5) Check her medicines for anticoagulants or antiplatelets. Give blood-clot prevention after surgery with low-molecular-weight heparin. Restart full anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation when the surgeons agree it is safe from a bleeding point of view. (6) Find out why she had a biliary stent (earlier ERCP and its reason) and refer her to gastroenterology or hepatobiliary to review drainage of her bile duct, since the stent has migrated. (7) Send the resected bowel to histopathology. (8) Arrange surgical outpatient follow-up in 2 weeks for wound and drain review.
